Research indicates that dogs do possess the ability to understand human language to a significant degree. [d3] A study using fMRI brain imaging found that dogs process words with their left hemisphere and intonation with their right hemisphere, similar to how humans process language, suggesting they can distinguish meaningful words from gibberish [d3]; a separate study published in NeuroImage confirmed that dogs can detect speech and distinguish languages without any explicit training, with some brain regions lighting up differently depending on whether the language is familiar or foreign [d2]. Dogs have been shown to understand hundreds of object names—Rico the border collie knew over 200 object names [d7], and Chaser knew the distinct names of 1,022 objects [d4]—and brain scans further revealed that dogs can combine word meaning and intonation for accurate interpretation, much like human brains do [d8]. While research is nuanced—some sources note that dogs may not fully grasp the abstract nature of human language [d9]—the overall picture is that dogs do comprehend human words to a meaningful extent, though to what degree depends on the individual dog's training and vocabulary size [d6][d1].
